idea:
Filter the pool down to clean, target-like (WikiText-style) documents, deduplicate, and shuffle.

1. Bigram fluency score. Split each text on whitespace. Split target_sample into halves A and B. Build the set of the 5000 most frequent word bigrams from A and score the B docs as the fraction of each doc's bigrams that are in the set; do the reverse for A. This gives held-out scores for all 200 target docs. Then build the final top-5000 bigram set from all 200 docs and score every pool doc the same way. This should catch word-shuffled articles (same unigrams, broken bigrams), spam and off-domain web text.

2. Threshold. Keep pool docs with score >= the 5th percentile of the held-out target scores, multiplied by 0.95 as a small correction for the larger final bigram set.

3. Junk guards. Drop docs with fewer than 200 characters. Drop docs whose share of non-ASCII characters, or of characters outside letters/digits/space/common punctuation, exceeds the maximum seen in target_sample times 1.5.

4. Deduplicate. Normalise by lowercasing and collapsing whitespace, then keep only the first doc for each hash of the full normalised text and also for each hash of its first 300 characters.

5. Order and fill. Shuffle the kept docs using CURATE_SEED and return them. If the kept tokens (estimated as chars/4) come to less than about 0.5 T, append the next-highest-scoring rejected, deduplicated docs until 0.5 T is reached. Otherwise let the trainer cycle the clean set.
why: The pool sample shows about half the documents are spam, word-shuffled articles, off-domain web text or duplicates, so spending all T tokens on clean in-domain wiki text should lower bpb substantially compared with the unfiltered pool.
outcome: dev 1.8306 against 1.9646 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Add a second, discriminative filter on top of the current pipeline; a doc must pass both. Keep the bigram threshold, junk guards, dedup, shuffle and 0.5 T fill unchanged.

1. Chunking. Split every text into consecutive 200-whitespace-word chunks, keeping a last chunk only if it has at least 50 words.

2. Training data (PU setup). Positives are all chunks of the 200 target_sample docs. Negatives are chunks of 4000 pool docs drawn at random with CURATE_SEED, capped at 5 chunks per doc.

3. Model. HashingVectorizer(analyzer='word', token_pattern=r'\S+', lowercase=False, ngram_range=(1,2), n_features=2**18, binary=True, norm='l2') followed by LogisticRegression(C=10, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=200).

4. Calibration. Run 5-fold cross-validation grouped by target doc to get held-out probabilities for the target chunks. Set thr_mean to the 5th percentile of the per-doc mean held-out probability, and thr_min to the 1st percentile of the held-out chunk probabilities.

5. Scoring. Score all chunks of every pool doc that passes the existing guards. Keep a doc only if it passes the existing bigram threshold, its mean chunk probability is at least thr_mean, and its minimum chunk probability is at least thr_min. The minimum test is there to drop articles that are only partly word-shuffled or have off-domain text spliced in.

6. Fill. If the 0.5 T fill is needed, rank the rejected docs by mean chunk probability instead of bigram score.

7. Time. If the 180 s budget is at risk, score only the first 10 chunks of each doc.
why: The top-5000 bigram fraction is a loose test that probably lets through fluent off-domain text and partly corrupted articles, while a classifier trained against the pool itself with a per-chunk minimum should give a purer target-style set for the 300 training steps.
outcome: dev 1.8288 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Keep the current pipeline (bigram threshold, junk guards, dedup, shuffle, 0.5 T fill) and add cheap structural damage guards, each calibrated on target_sample. A doc must pass all of them before dedup.

1. Compression ratio. Compute r = len(zlib.compress(text.encode('utf-8'), 6)) / len(bytes) on the first 20,000 characters. Keep docs with r between (min target r) * 0.93 and (max target r) * 1.05. The low bound drops docs with internally repeated paragraphs or boilerplate; the high bound drops character-noise or garbled docs.

2. Repeated lines. Among non-empty lines longer than 40 characters, compute the share that are exact repeats of an earlier line in the same doc. Drop the doc if this share exceeds max(target max * 1.5, 0.05).

3. Character-class shares. Compute the uppercase-letter share, digit share and whitespace share of all characters. Drop docs outside [target min * 0.7, target max * 1.3] on any of the three. This catches all-caps, lowercased, number-table and space-stripped docs.

4. Local bigram fluency. Split the doc into consecutive 150-word windows, keeping a last window only if it has at least 75 words, and score each window with the existing final bigram set. Calibrate with the existing A/B half split: compute each target doc's held-out minimum window score and set thr_win to the 2nd percentile of those minima times 0.95. Drop pool docs whose minimum window score is below thr_win. This catches articles that are only partly word-shuffled or have junk spliced in.

5. Stronger dedup. In addition to the full-text and 300-character prefix hashes, hash the normalised characters 1000 to 1300 (when the doc is long enough) and the last 300 characters. Treat a doc as a duplicate if its full-text hash, its prefix hash or its middle hash has been seen, or if its suffix hash has been seen together with the same first line (title).

Fill and shuffle stay unchanged, and fill candidates must also pass guards 1 to 3.
why: The whole-doc bigram mean cannot see partly shuffled, internally repeated, case-damaged or near-duplicate articles, and removing them should clean up the cycled training set without the cost of the rejected classifier.
outcome: dev 1.8345 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Remove the low-quality fill and train on the clean set only, repeated with a fresh shuffle each pass. Keep steps 1 to 4 (bigram threshold, junk guards, dedup) exactly as they are.

1. Count tokens exactly. Use tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch) on the kept docs only, instead of the chars/4 estimate.

2. Lower the fill floor. Replace FILL_FRACTION = 0.5 with a safety floor of 0.08 T. Only if the clean, deduplicated kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, append the highest-scoring rejected deduplicated docs until 0.08 T is reached. Otherwise add no rejected docs at all.

3. Build the output explicitly. Shuffle the kept list with random.Random(seed) and append it. Repeat with a new shuffle from the same RNG for each further pass, until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of margin. The trainer then never cycles in a fixed order, and every pass contains only clean in-domain docs.
why: The pool sample suggests clean target-style articles are scarce, so the 0.5 T fill is probably feeding in word-shuffled or damaged near-miss docs, and for a 300-step model a second pass over clean in-domain text should beat that.
outcome: dev 1.8243 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Combine the clean-only multi-pass output of experiment 4 (which measured 1.8243) with topic weighting towards the target sample, so that the extra passes are spent on the most target-like clean docs instead of uniform repeats. Keep steps 1 to 4 (bigram threshold, junk guards, dedup) exactly as they are.

1. Exact token counts. Count tokens of the kept docs with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch). Replace the 0.5 T fill with a safety floor of 0.08 T: append the highest-scoring rejected deduplicated docs only if the kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens.

2. Topic similarity. Fit TfidfVectorizer(lowercase=True, token_pattern=r"[A-Za-z]{3,}", sublinear_tf=True, min_df=3, max_features=50000, norm='l2') on the kept docs plus target_sample. Compute sim[i] as the cosine between kept doc i and the L2-normalised mean TF-IDF vector of the 200 target docs. Convert sim to a rank percentile p[i] in [0,1] among the kept docs.

3. Pass construction.
   - Pass 1: all kept docs, shuffled with random.Random(seed).
   - Each later pass k = 2, 3, ...: include doc i with probability 0.25 + 0.75 * p[i], using the same RNG, then shuffle the pass.
   - Add passes until the cumulative exact token count reaches T.

4. Final segment. Build the last 0.15 T tokens of the output only from docs with p[i] >= 0.5, shuffled, so that the low-learning-rate end of training sees the most target-like text. To do this, truncate the pass list at 0.85 T tokens and then append shuffled top-half docs until the total is at least T plus a small margin.

5. Return the concatenated list. It must be at least T tokens long so the trainer never cycles.
why: Dropping the junk fill already measured lower (1.8243), and the target sample looks topically concentrated (military history), so spending the repeated passes and the end of training on the most target-similar clean docs should add a gain large enough to clear the noise.
outcome: dev 1.8297 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Combine the two changes that each moved dev in the right direction (experiment 4's clean-only multi-pass output at 1.8243 and experiment 2's discriminative filter at 1.8288). Keep steps 1 to 4 (bigram threshold, junk guards, dedup) as they are.

1. Discriminative filter, as in experiment 2. Split texts into 200-whitespace-word chunks, keeping a last chunk only if it has at least 50 words. Positives are all chunks of target_sample. Negatives are chunks of 4000 pool docs drawn at random with CURATE_SEED, capped at 5 chunks per doc. Model: HashingVectorizer(analyzer='word', token_pattern=r'\S+', lowercase=False, ngram_range=(1,2), n_features=2**18, binary=True, norm='l2') followed by LogisticRegression(C=10, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=200).

2. Calibration. Run 5-fold cross-validation grouped by target doc to get held-out probabilities for the target chunks. Set thr_mean to the 5th percentile of the per-doc mean held-out probability and thr_min to the 1st percentile of the held-out chunk probabilities.

3. Scoring. To save time, score only pool docs that already pass the guards and the bigram threshold, and only their first 10 chunks. Keep a doc only if its mean chunk probability is at least thr_mean and its minimum chunk probability is at least thr_min. Apply this before dedup, so that a damaged copy cannot shadow a clean duplicate.

4. Dedup. Among duplicates (same full-text hash or same 300-character prefix hash), keep the copy with the highest mean chunk probability instead of the first occurrence.

5. Clean-only output, as in experiment 4. Count tokens of the kept docs exactly with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch). Remove the 0.5 T fill. Only if the kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, append the rejected deduplicated docs with the highest mean chunk probability until 0.08 T is reached.

6. Passes. Build the output as repeated passes over the kept set, each with a fresh shuffle from random.Random(seed), until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of margin. The trainer then never cycles in a fixed order and never sees fill docs.
why: Experiments 2 and 4 each gave a small gain from a different source (stricter in-domain purity, and no low-quality fill with reshuffled passes), so stacking them and letting the cleanest duplicate win may add up to a gain large enough to be accepted.
outcome: dev 1.8295 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Build on experiment 4's clean-only multi-pass output (the lowest dev so far, 1.8243) and add a rare-word damage guard, which has not been tried. Keep the bigram score and threshold, the junk guards and the dedup rule as they are.

1. Pool vocabulary. Split every pool doc on whitespace and compute the document frequency of each word (case-sensitive) over the whole pool. Call a word "rare" if its document frequency is 2 or less.

2. Rare-word rate. For each doc, compute rare_rate = (number of word tokens that are rare) / (number of word tokens). For target_sample docs, use the same pool document frequencies; a word absent from the pool counts as rare.

3. Calibrate. Set max_rare = (95th percentile of the target docs' rare_rate) * 1.5 + 0.005. Drop any pool doc with rare_rate > max_rare. This is aimed at docs with character noise, typos, glued or split words, or garbled encoding. Such docs can still pass the bigram threshold when their original score was high.

4. Local guard. Compute rare_rate on consecutive 200-word windows, keeping a last window only if it has at least 100 words. Drop the doc if any window exceeds max_win, where max_win = (99th percentile of all target window rare_rates) * 2 + 0.01. This catches docs damaged in only one part.

5. Dedup order. Apply both guards before dedup, so a damaged copy cannot shadow a clean duplicate. Among duplicates (same full-text hash or same 300-character prefix hash), keep the copy with the lowest rare_rate, breaking ties by the higher bigram score.

6. Output, as in experiment 4. Count tokens of the kept docs exactly with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch). Remove the 0.5 T fill. Only if the kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, append the highest-scoring rejected deduplicated docs that pass the rare-word guards until 0.08 T is reached. Build the output as repeated passes over the kept set, each with a fresh shuffle from random.Random(seed), until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of margin.
why: The absolute bigram threshold lets through lightly damaged copies of high-scoring articles, and a rare-word rate measured against the pool's own vocabulary should catch that noise directly, while the clean-only reshuffled passes keep the one change that measured best so far.
outcome: dev 1.8301 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Start from experiment 4's clean-only multi-pass output (exact tiktoken counts, no 0.5 T fill, 0.08 T safety floor only, fresh shuffle per pass until T plus one pass of margin) and raise recall of clean target-format articles by replacing the fixed percentile threshold with a valley threshold for docs that look like target articles.

1. Header test. Mark a doc as 'article-format' if its first line matches ^= [^=].* =$ (the same title format as the target sample). Junk guards and the bigram score are unchanged.

2. Valley threshold. Take the bigram scores of all article-format pool docs that pass the guards. They should be bimodal: clean articles high, word-shuffled copies low. Find the split with 1-D 2-means (initialise the centres at the 10th and 90th percentiles, run 20 iterations) and set thr_valley to the midpoint of the two centres. Set thr_article = min(current threshold, max(thr_valley, 0.6 * current threshold)). If the two centres differ by less than 0.05, use thr_article = current threshold.

3. Selection. Keep article-format docs with score >= thr_article. Keep all other docs only if score >= the current threshold (5th percentile of held-out target scores times 0.95), as now.

4. Dedup. Process candidates in descending bigram score instead of pool order, so that among copies with the same full-text hash or the same 300-character prefix hash the most fluent copy is kept.

5. Output. Build the passes as in experiment 4.
why: The fixed 5th-percentile cut-off discards at least 5% of clean in-domain articles by construction, while shuffled copies probably score far lower, so a valley threshold should recover unique clean target text at little risk and add it to the clean-only multi-pass output that gave the lowest dev so far.
outcome: dev 1.8210 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Rebuild experiment 8 (the lowest dev so far, 1.8210) and add title-based dedup plus an article-format-only kept set.

1. Scoring and guards. Keep the bigram score, the held-out threshold (5th percentile of held-out target scores times 0.95) and the junk guards (200-character minimum, non-ASCII share, odd-character share) as they are.

2. Header test. Mark a doc as 'article-format' if its first line, stripped, matches ^= [^=].* =$.

3. Valley threshold, as in experiment 8. Take the bigram scores of article-format pool docs that pass the guards. Run 1-D 2-means (centres initialised at the 10th and 90th percentiles, 20 iterations). Set thr_valley to the midpoint of the two centres and thr_article = min(current threshold, max(thr_valley, 0.6 * current threshold)). If the centres differ by less than 0.05, use thr_article = current threshold.

4. Selection. Candidates are article-format docs with score >= thr_article. Non-article-format docs are not kept, even if they pass the current threshold. They are used only for the safety floor in step 6.

5. Dedup. Process candidates in descending bigram score, breaking ties by index. Skip a doc if any of these has been seen: its full-text hash, its 300-character prefix hash, or its title key. The title key is the first line, lowercased and whitespace-collapsed. This keeps one copy per article title, the most fluent one, and removes lightly damaged or perturbed copies that differ in the prefix and so escape the hash dedup.

6. Output, as in experiment 4. Count tokens of the kept docs exactly with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch). Do not use the 0.5 T fill. Only if the kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, append the highest-scoring remaining deduplicated docs (non-article docs that pass the current threshold first, then rejected docs) until 0.08 T is reached. Build the output as repeated passes over the kept set, each with a fresh shuffle from random.Random(seed), until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of margin.
why: Experiment 8's recall gain gave the lowest dev so far, and one-copy-per-title dedup plus dropping non-article docs should remove the remaining damaged near-duplicate copies and off-format text that the hash dedup and the bigram threshold let through.
outcome: dev 1.8293 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Rebuild experiment 8 (the lowest dev so far, 1.8210) and add one self-training round that rescores the whole pool with a much larger bigram model, to raise recall of clean target-style docs.

1. Stage A (seed set). Run experiment 8's selection unchanged: junk guards, top-5000 target bigram score, the held-out threshold (5th percentile times 0.95), the 2-means valley threshold for article-format docs (first line matches ^= [^=].* =$), and dedup in descending score on the full-text hash and the 300-character prefix hash. Call the result S.

2. Stage B (bigger fluency model). Count word bigrams (whitespace split) over all docs in S plus target_sample. Take the 100,000 most frequent as set B2. Score every guard-passing pool doc and every target_sample doc as the fraction of its bigrams that are in B2.

3. Calibrate. The target docs are not in the pool, so their B2 scores are effectively held out. Set thr2 = (3rd percentile of the target B2 scores) * 0.95.

4. Final selection. Keep every guard-passing pool doc with B2 score >= thr2, whatever its header format. Also keep any doc of S whose B2 score is at least 0.9 * thr2. Do not apply the stage-A threshold to the other docs.

5. Dedup. Process candidates in descending B2 score, ties by index. Skip a doc if its full-text hash or its 300-character prefix hash has been seen. Do not dedup on title.

6. Output, as in experiment 4. Count tokens exactly with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch). Do not use the 0.5 T fill. Only if the kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, append the docs with the highest B2 scores among the rest until 0.08 T is reached. Build repeated passes over the kept set, each with a fresh shuffle from random.Random(seed), until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of margin.

7. Time. If the 180 s budget is at risk, count and score bigrams on the first 3000 words of each doc only.
why: The 200-doc, 5000-bigram scorer probably under-scores clean articles on unusual topics and headerless fragments, and experiments 8 and 9 hint that more distinct clean target-style text helps, so a bigger bigram model built from the kept set and calibrated on the target sample should recover more of it while still rejecting shuffled and off-domain docs.
outcome: dev 1.8258 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Rebuild experiment 8 (the lowest dev so far, 1.8210) and change only how the passes are composed, so that non-article text is seen once, early, and the rest of training is target-format articles only.

1. Selection, unchanged from experiment 8. Keep the junk guards, the top-5000 target bigram score and the held-out threshold (5th percentile of held-out target scores times 0.95). Mark a doc 'article-format' if its first line, stripped, matches ^= [^=].* =$. Compute the 2-means valley threshold on the article-format scores (centres initialised at the 10th and 90th percentiles, 20 iterations; thr_article = min(current threshold, max(midpoint, 0.6 * current threshold)); fall back to the current threshold if the centres differ by less than 0.05). Keep article-format docs with score >= thr_article and other docs with score >= the current threshold. Dedup in descending bigram score (ties by index) on the full-text hash and the 300-character prefix hash. Do not dedup on title.

2. Split the kept set into A (article-format) and N (not article-format). Count tokens exactly with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch).

3. Output.
   - Pass 1: A plus N together, shuffled with random.Random(seed).
   - Pass 2 onwards: A only, with a fresh shuffle from the same RNG for each pass, until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of A as margin.
   - If pass 1 alone already exceeds T tokens, reorder it: put all of N, mixed with a random subset of A of equal token size, first, and the remaining A docs after, so that the docs cut off at T tokens come from the mixed front part as little as possible and the tail of training is pure A.
   - If A has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, fall back to experiment 8's output exactly (all kept docs in every pass, with the 0.08 T safety floor fill).

4. No 0.5 T fill and no other changes.
why: Experiment 8's selection gave the lowest dev, and spending every repeat pass and the low-learning-rate end of training only on target-format articles (while still seeing the other fluent text once) should move the trained distribution closer to the held-out articles without the diversity loss that hurt experiment 9; note that experiments 4 to 10 all landed between 1.821 and 1.830, so differences this small may be single-run noise.
outcome: dev 1.8293 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Rebuild experiment 8 exactly (the lowest dev so far, 1.8210) and add only a title-based near-duplicate dedup for article-format docs. Non-article docs stay in the kept set, unlike experiment 9.

1. Selection, unchanged from experiment 8. Keep the junk guards (200-character minimum, non-ASCII share, odd-character share), the top-5000 target bigram score and the held-out threshold (5th percentile of held-out target scores times 0.95). Mark a doc 'article-format' if its first line, stripped, matches ^= [^=].* =$. Compute the 2-means valley threshold on the article-format scores of guard-passing docs (centres initialised at the 10th and 90th percentiles, 20 iterations). Set thr_article = min(current threshold, max(midpoint, 0.6 * current threshold)), falling back to the current threshold if the centres differ by less than 0.05. Keep article-format docs with score >= thr_article and all other docs with score >= the current threshold.

2. Dedup. Process candidates in descending bigram score, ties by index. Skip a doc if its full-text hash or its 300-character prefix hash has been seen. New: for article-format docs only, also skip the doc if its title key has been seen. The title key is the first line, lowercased and whitespace-collapsed. This keeps exactly one copy per article title, the most fluent one. It removes lightly perturbed, truncated or partly shuffled copies of an article that differ in the first 300 characters and so escape the hash dedup. Non-article docs are deduped by the two hashes only.

3. Output, as in experiments 4 and 8. Count tokens of the kept docs exactly with tiktoken "gpt2" (encode_ordinary_batch). Do not use the 0.5 T fill. Only if the kept set has fewer than 0.08 T tokens, append the highest-scoring remaining deduplicated docs until 0.08 T is reached. Build the output as repeated passes over the kept set, each with a fresh shuffle from random.Random(seed), until the cumulative token count reaches T plus one pass of margin.
why: Experiment 8's lowered article threshold probably lets in lower-scoring damaged copies of articles whose clean copy is already kept, and a per-title dedup removes them without dropping the non-article docs as experiment 9 did; I expect at most a gain of the size of the run-to-run spread seen so far (about 0.005 bpb).
outcome: dev 1.8300 against 1.8306 for the best at the time, rejected
